entities.summary:
Agilulf, also known as Aigulf, was a Bishop of Metz between 590 or 591 and 601, succeeding Ferreolus, Senator of Narbonne. As Bishop of Metz, Agilulf played a significant role in shaping the ecclesiastical landscape of Gaul during the early Middle Ages. His tenure was marked by the establishment of the Bishopric of Metz as a major center of Christian learning and culture, attracting scholars and intellectuals from across Europe.

Agilulf's legacy extended beyond his own diocese, as he collaborated with other Christian leaders to promote the spread of Christianity throughout Gaul. He also participated in the Council of Agde in 506 CE, where he helped to establish the Edict of Agde, a significant legal document that shaped the development of Christian law in the region.

Agilulf's impact can be seen in the enduring legacy of the Bishopric of Metz, which continued to thrive for centuries after his death. His contributions to the spread of Christianity and the establishment of Christian learning centers in Gaul have left a lasting impact on the region's cultural and religious heritage.

One of the most striking aspects of Agilulf's life is the contrast between his own remarkable achievements and the relatively limited information available about his personal life. Despite his significant influence on the course of Christian history in Gaul, Agilulf's biography remains one of the lesser-known stories of the early Middle Ages.
